messages.subject: Re: cluster size?
parts:
I am currently utilising Distance sampling on kangaroos, which some of
you may know form very large groups (up to 60 in some instances). I
define a group based on Colin Southwell's work and that is animals that
are detected less than 50m from each other and able to maintain visual
contact. Now these groups may comprise several biological groups (mother
and young-at-foot, sub-adults and dominant males) but they are all
considered one large group because they are all sighted together. I
think it is also important that you keep the definition of the group
consistent throughout the study period.

Hope this helps
Kind regards
Michael

>>> >>> Jeff Laake <jeff....@NOAA.GOV> 21/10/2004 5:05:01 am >>>
This is a difficult problem because it can be viewed as either
dependent
detections or underestimating group size. It is important to
recognize
that a group for distance sampling may not be a group from a
biological
stand point. As I view it, a "group" is a collection of animals that
are sighted together. If as you describe, birds are detected
independently even though they are in close proximity, I would treat
them as separate observations. Then I would also explore a bootstrap
variance approach to guard against underestimating the variance due to
dependence in detections.

Any other thoughts out there?

--jeff
